claims.plain: Being the decision-maker is unpleasant in itself, whether or not the partner ends up worse off.
The drop in happiness after a partner's bad outcome is disappointment at the participant's own outcome, not guilt.
The imaging pipeline fails to recover known effects, so the Social-Partner differences cannot be credited to the manipulation.
The model-based fMRI approach recovers no known neural signals, so regressors from the computational model cannot be trusted.
Participants chose inattentively or at random, so their choices say nothing about what they preferred or felt.
Choosing for someone else changes how much risk people accept, and that, not guilt, explains the differences between conditions.
On one fit measure, the Responsibility Redux model fitted momentary happiness best in both studies.
The anterior insula carries the guilt effect, responding more when the participant is responsible for the partner's bad outcome.
The anterior insula should respond more in the Social than the Partner condition, and most strongly after low outcomes.
The left superior temporal sulcus tracks a partner's surprising outcomes less when the participant did not cause them.
The larger drop in happiness after a partner's bad outcome that the participant caused fits the idea of simple guilt.
The ventral striatum on both sides was more active when participants chose the risky option, in every condition, as found before.
In both studies participants felt worse after a partner's bad outcome they had chosen, which the authors read as guilt.
Connectivity from the left insula and left superior temporal sulcus to prefrontal cortex should depend on condition and choice.
The right inferior frontal gyrus, in its coupling with the left anterior insula, is sensitive to guilt during social choices.
Deciding for both players rather than alone engaged the precuneus, left temporo-parietal junction and medial prefrontal cortex.
The gap between low and high outcome responses was larger in the Social condition in both insulae and middle temporal cortex.
Individual neural guilt responses matched a previously published guilt brain signature, converging with earlier work.
At outcome both insulae responded more, and right middle temporal cortex less, to low outcomes in Social than Partner trials.
Lottery rather than safe outcomes engaged the anterior insula, ventral striatum, dmPFC, right STS and frontoparietal cortex.
On each trial participants chose between a safe and a risky option, for themselves, for both players, or the partner chose.
The findings rest on two samples of healthy adults, one behavioural and one scanned, with all brain results from the scanner.
Coupling between the guilt- and responsibility-related regions and prefrontal cortex changes with who decides and what is chosen.
Left anterior insula coupling with the right inferior frontal gyrus was strongest for risky self choices and safe joint choices.
The guilt effect held whether the participant's own lottery outcome was high or low.
The partner's choices were simulated by an algorithm always taking the highest expected value, the same for every participant.
The neural guilt signature did not track how strongly individual participants showed the behavioural guilt effect.
The insula responded more to a partner's low outcome when the participant had chosen, mirroring the behavioural guilt effect.
A left inferior frontal gyrus cluster showed the opposite coupling pattern with the left STS seed, but did not survive correction.
A smaller left inferior frontal gyrus cluster showed the same insula coupling pattern as the right, but did not survive correction.
The left superior temporal sulcus tracked the participant's reward predictions from both participant and partner choices.
The Responsibility model fitted the happiness data better than every other model, including Responsibility Redux.
The happiness model with all three two-way interactions fitted better than simpler models and no worse than the fullest one.
Being the decision-maker may itself cost happiness, a weight of responsibility.
As a check, ventral striatum activity on both sides rose with the rewards participants expected from their chosen option.
A small left anterior insula cluster responded more to a partner's low outcome after the participant's own choice.
Choosing for both players raised the rate of risky choices in the first study but not in the second.
A model-based analysis used the fitted model's reward and prediction-error terms to locate the brain regions reflecting them.
Model selection compared the Responsibility model against each rival model in turn, alongside the usual fit criteria.
Momentary happiness was fitted with five computational models sharing decaying terms for rewards, expectations and surprises.
Regions sensitive to risky outcomes should respond more to a partner's reward surprises when the participant caused them.
A brain region tracks responsibility, representing a partner's reward surprises more strongly when the participant chose.
Sensitivity to the value difference between the options did not change across conditions in either study.
A left superior temporal sulcus cluster responded more to the partner's reward surprises after the participant's own choices.
Only the precuneus and temporo-parietal junction were most active when participants chose the lottery for both players.
Fitting the happiness model to simulated data recovered its parameters reliably, showing the estimates are stable.
Participants were less happy when they were the one deciding, whatever the outcome.
Among the influences on momentary happiness is the reward the partner received on the current trial.
Among the influences on momentary happiness is the reward the participant received on the current trial.
One measure of risk taking, how often the lottery was chosen, was higher deciding alone than for both, in the first study only.
Participants' own reward surprises shaped their happiness more than their partner's did.
Participants chose the lottery more often the more its expected value exceeded the safe option.
Risk preferences were much the same whether deciding alone or for both players, with only a hint of extra caution for both.
A second risk measure, the fitted risk-aversion parameter, was slightly higher deciding for both than alone in Study 1 only.
The partner's reward surprises that followed the participant's own choices helped explain the participant's momentary happiness.
A pre-task icebreaker left participants rating their partners highly on every likeability measure in both studies.
Earlier connectivity work linked social choice, guilt compensation and responsibility aversion to distinct network interactions.
Earlier work links the anterior insula to guilt.
Responsibility made no difference to happiness after good outcomes for the partner, bounding the effect to bad ones.
On explained variance, the Responsibility model beat every rival except the Guilt-envy model in the first study.
Happiness should fall further after a partner's low outcome when the participant rather than the partner chose the lottery.
A happiness model including the partner's surprises from the participant's own choices should fit better than models without them.
The Responsibility Redux model, built from both players' rewards, surprises and who decided, predicted momentary happiness well.
Responsibility for a choice that leaves a partner worse off produces guilt, felt as a sharper drop in the chooser's happiness.
Risk aversion was the same on gain and loss trials, so the two could be pooled.
A third risk measure, the risk premium, was the same whether participants decided alone or for both players.
Earlier work established that momentary happiness in a reward task follows recent expectations and the surprises against them.
Set against the partner deciding, choosing the lottery raised the response in precuneus, mPFC and left TPJ and lowered it in ventral striatum.
Set against deciding alone, choosing the lottery raised the response in precuneus and left TPJ and lowered it in ventral striatum and mPFC.
Study 2 repeated the Study 1 design in the scanner, with longer gaps between trials and experimenters as partners.
After a partner's low outcome, participants were less happy when they rather than the partner had chosen the lottery.
